topic: Learning mode: why answering beats re-reading
oneSentenceAnswer: Re-reading a page feels like learning; answering questions about it is what actually keeps the page in your head a week later.
fiveMinutePath: Try the three questions at the top before you know any answers.
Read the key ideas, four at a time, not ten.
Answer each check, then open the feedback.
Compare what you guessed at the start with what you learned.
Come back on day 1, day 3 and day 7.
whyItMatters: Testing yourself beats re-reading on any delayed test.
Two techniques carry most of the benefit: self-testing and spacing.
A page that only looks good teaches less than one that asks.

keyIdeas.title: Pulling a fact out changes it
keyIdeas.body: Five minutes after studying, re-reading wins. Two days and a week later, the group that was tested remembers far more. Retrieval is not a measurement of learning, it is an act of learning.

keyIdeas.title: Most study tricks are weak
keyIdeas.body: A review of ten common techniques rated only two as high utility: practice testing and distributed practice. Highlighting, summarising and re-reading were rated low.

keyIdeas.title: Questions before reading, not only after
keyIdeas.body: Asking a question the reader cannot yet answer helps the material that question names. It does almost nothing for the rest of the page, so ask about what must stick.

keyIdeas.title: Four new things, not seven
keyIdeas.body: When grouping and rehearsal are blocked, working memory holds about three to five items. A block that introduces ten at once is a block the reader will not hold.

keyIdeas.title: Feedback comes after the answer
keyIdeas.body: Retrieval works without feedback and works better with it, mainly by correcting confident mistakes. Printing the answer under the question removes the retrieval and keeps none of the benefit.

diagrams.alt: A loop: ask before reading, read a short block, answer a check, open the feedback, then revisit on day 1, 3 and 7.
diagrams.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Ask first] --> B[Read one block]
  B --> C[Answer a check]
  C --> D[Open the feedback]
  D --> E[Revisit D1 D3 D7]
  E --> B

examples.title: The same page, one week apart
examples.body: Two readers finish this page. One re-reads it twice. One closes it and writes down what they remember. On day seven the second reader recalls noticeably more of it.

examples.title: A question that teaches nothing
examples.body: Ask "is spacing better than cramming?" with the options "yes" and "no" and everyone scores full marks. The page now feels mastered and nothing was retrieved.

analogies.setup: A memory is a path through a field. Reading about the path is watching someone else walk it.
analogies.takeaway: Every time you walk it yourself, the grass stays flat a little longer.

misconceptions.myth: If the page feels easy, I have learned it.
misconceptions.truth: Ease of reading is fluency, and fluency reliably makes people overconfident. An easy quiz adds fluency instead of correcting it.

misconceptions.myth: Points and badges will make people learn more.
misconceptions.truth: Rewards tied to engagement or completion reduced intrinsic motivation across 128 studies. What helps is feedback that shows competence, not the token itself.

glossary.definition: Answering from memory instead of re-reading. The answering is what strengthens the memory.
A question asked before the reading, which the reader is expected to get wrong.
Spreading revision over separate days rather than repeating it once in one sitting.
The feeling that material is easy. It tracks how smooth the text is, not how much you will remember.
A sentence with words removed, which the reader fills back in from memory.

practicalTakeaways: Put two or three questions at the top of anything you want remembered.
Give every key idea one question whose answer is not in its own prompt.
Say why the right answer is right, and show it only after the reader commits.
Plan a day 1, day 3 and day 7 pass instead of one long session.

sourceMap.title: Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention
sourceMap.summary: After 5 minutes repeated studying wins; on delayed tests at 2 days and 1 week prior testing produces substantially greater retention.
claims: retrieval beats restudy at a delay

sourceMap.title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques
sourceMap.publisher: Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1), 4-58
sourceMap.summary: Ten techniques rated on four criteria: only practice testing and distributed practice are rated high utility; highlighting and rereading are rated low.
claims: only two of ten techniques rate high utility

sourceMap.title: Prequestioning and Pretesting Effects: a Review of Empirical Research, Theoretical Perspectives, and Implications for Educational Practice
sourceMap.summary: Prequestions help the specifically prequestioned material (g about 0.66) and not the rest of the passage (g about 0.01).
claims: prequestions help only what they ask about

sourceMap.title: The magical number 4 in short-term memory: a reconsideration of mental storage capacity
sourceMap.summary: Across paradigms that block chunking and rehearsal, the capacity limit is closer to 3-5 items than to Miller's seven.

sourceMap.title: The critical role of retrieval practice in long-term retention
sourceMap.summary: Retrieval produces benefits without feedback and larger benefits with it, particularly by correcting high-confidence errors.
claims: feedback after the answer increases the retrieval benefit

sourceMap.title: Illusions of Competence in Monitoring One's Knowledge During Study
sourceMap.summary: Learners systematically overestimate what they will remember when the answer is in front of them during study.

sourceMap.title: A Meta-Analytic Review of Experiments Examining the Effects of Extrinsic Rewards on Intrinsic Motivation
sourceMap.summary: Across 128 studies, engagement-, completion- and performance-contingent rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d = -0.40, -0.36, -0.28); positive feedback raised it.

uncertaintyNotes: Effect sizes here come from meta-analyses of classroom and laboratory studies, mostly with students. Nobody has measured a one-page web explainer specifically.
The day 1 / day 3 / day 7 prompts are a reasonable default for a short horizon, not an optimal schedule. The best gap grows with how long you need to remember.

prequestions.question: A week after reading, who remembers more: the reader who re-read twice, or the reader who tested themselves once?
prequestions.hint: Ask yourself which one felt harder at the time.

prequestions.question: How many genuinely new things can you hold at once while reading?
prequestions.hint: The famous number is wrong in the direction you would not expect.

prequestions.question: Why is a quiz everyone passes a bad quiz?
prequestions.hint: Think about what the score is really measuring.

checks.prompt: Roediger and Karpicke tested readers 5 minutes, 2 days and 1 week after study. What changed with the delay?
options: Repeated study stayed ahead at every delay
Prior testing overtook repeated study on the delayed tests
The two groups were level at all three delays
checks.why: At 5 minutes restudy was ahead. At 2 days and 1 week the tested group retained substantially more, which is why immediate performance is a poor guide.

checks.prompt: Of the ten study techniques reviewed in 2013, how many earned a high utility rating?
checks.why: Only practice testing and distributed practice. Summarising, highlighting, the keyword mnemonic, imagery and rereading were rated low utility.

checks.prompt: You open a page with three questions. What do they improve?
options: Everything in the page that follows
Only the material those three questions are about
Nothing, because the reader gets them wrong
checks.why: The benefit is close to g = 0.66 for the prequestioned material and close to zero for the rest, so prequestions have to name what must stick.

checks.prompt: How many new items should one block of a page introduce at once?
options: As many as fit on screen
checks.why: When chunking and rehearsal are blocked, capacity sits near three to five items. Miller's seven was offered as a rhetorical figure, not a measured limit.

cloze.text: Immediate performance is ___ ; what you keep after a ___ is learning.
Feedback belongs ___ the answer, never ___ it.

revision.d1: Close the page and list the five key ideas from memory. Then check.
revision.d3: Redo the four checks. Note only the ones you got wrong.
revision.d7: Explain to someone why re-reading feels better than it works.
